---
title: "Talking to patients about AI"
subtitle: "AIM-6 · AIM-4 · about one hour"
---

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will have:

1. Written, and improved with a chatbot's help, what you will say when a
   patient asks about a tool in the room: what they can refuse, what they
   cannot, and what you do not know.
2. Told a patient what an AI tool did, what a person did, and who is
   responsible, as three separate sentences.
3. Practised, with a chatbot playing the patient, answering someone who brings
   chatbot output that is partly right, without giving in and without talking
   down to them.
4. Explained why text that raters call more empathetic can still persuade
   patients less than a person does.
5. Kept a set of sentences to say out loud at your Friday small group.
:::

**Time.** About 15 minutes of reading, 40 minutes of doing, and five minutes
at the end. The podcast is optional. Use your university ChatGPT Edu or
Microsoft Copilot account; any free chatbot also works. There is nothing to
install, and nothing in this chapter involves a real patient.

## Two printed pages and a phone on the desk

It is your third week of intern year, in the continuity clinic. The patient is
34, a software developer, here for six weeks of fatigue. Labs from the first
visit were normal. She sits down, looks at the phone propped on the desk,
and asks, "Is that recording us?"

It is. The clinic went live last month with a tool that listens to the visit and
drafts the note, and you were told to use it. You start to answer, and she
slides two printed pages across the desk. "I ran my symptoms through ChatGPT.
I'd like these tests."

::: {.press-clip}
<div class="src">Printed from a general-purpose chatbot · illustrative, written for this chapter</div>
<p><b>Six weeks of fatigue in a 34-year-old with normal basic labs: what could be going on</b></p>
<p>Based on what you've described, the most likely explanations are <b>iron deficiency</b> (common even with a normal hemoglobin), <b>thyroid dysfunction</b>, <b>a sleep disorder</b>, and <b>depression or burnout</b>. Less common but worth ruling out: Addison's disease, Lyme disease, Epstein-Barr reactivation, heavy-metal exposure, and autoimmune disease.</p>
<p><b>Tests to ask your doctor for:</b> ferritin, TSH and free T4, morning cortisol, ANA, Lyme serology, EBV panel, heavy-metal screen, vitamin D, and a sleep study.</p>
<p><b>What you can do now:</b> start an over-the-counter iron supplement (325 mg daily) while you wait for results, since iron deficiency is the most likely cause and supplementation is low-risk.</p>
<p><i>This is general information and not a substitute for medical advice.</i></p>
:::

Read the two pages the way she did. About a third is reasonable: ferritin,
thyroid function, a sleep history, and a depression screen are exactly where
you were going. A third is testing for things she has no reason to have. And
the last paragraph tells her to start a drug before anyone has measured
whether she needs it.

She is not embarrassed and she is not hostile, and the phone is still
listening. You have perhaps ninety seconds to answer both questions, in the right order,
without losing her trust. That is the whole chapter.

If you would rather practise first and read after, go to [Part B of the
Do](#part-b-practice-patient) now. Then come back.

## Why this matters

![Every conversation in this chapter happens across a desk like this one, and
the tool is either on the desk, in the chart, or in the patient's hand. Photo:
National Cancer Institute, public domain (US federal government work), via
[Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Doctor_talking_with_a_patient.jpg).](../images/doctor-talking-with-patient.jpg){#fig-desk fig-alt="A physician in a white coat sits across a desk from a patient, both facing each other in conversation, with paperwork between them."}

You will need this in your first month. A tool will listen to your visits. A
draft of your portal reply will be written before you open the message. A
patient will bring you a printout.

Published lists of what physicians should know about AI (called competency
frameworks) name this skill [@pmid:36731054; @pmid:42120544]. Yet a review of
the training programs that exist found it covered in about one in five of the
papers describing them [@pmid:39023999]. One reason is that it cannot be
taught by lecture. The skill is not knowing what to say. It is saying it to a
person who is frightened, or skeptical, or already convinced the chatbot was
right.

That makes it a good place to use a chatbot well. It can play the patient,
point out your jargon, and tell you the order you spoke in. Then you say the
words to a person, which is what Friday is for.

## How it works

### More empathetic on the page, less persuasive in the room

Ask students what goes wrong when a machine talks to a patient, and the answer
is coldness. The evidence says otherwise. In 2023 a team took 195 patient
questions from a public forum where verified physicians answer, and had a
chatbot answer them too. Clinician raters, not told which answer was which,
compared the two [@pmid:37115527].

![Blinded raters preferred the chatbot's answer 78.6 percent of the time.
Redrawn from the abstract of Ayers et al., *JAMA Internal Medicine* 2023;
data are not copyrightable, drawing by the course.](../images/ayers-2023-redrawn.svg){#fig-ayers fig-alt="Three pairs of horizontal bars comparing physician and chatbot responses. Rated good or very good quality: physician 22.1 percent, chatbot 78.5 percent. Rated empathetic or very empathetic: physician 4.6 percent, chatbot 45.1 percent. Median length in words: physician 52, chatbot 211."}

As @fig-ayers shows, the chatbot's answers were rated more empathetic nearly
ten times as often, and were four times longer. A 2025 repeat with 1,454 lay
participants found the same ordering. The chatbot's answers contained more
validation, more reassurance, and more non-judgmental language, and read as
less rushed [@pmid:41359230]. Those are behaviors a person can learn. But this
is text judged by readers, with no relationship and no follow-up, against
physicians answering strangers for free.

The second finding favors the person. In a Zurich course, 52 medical students
watched four short pieces on the same treatment. They came from a patient, a
clinician, an expert, and ChatGPT, whose text was read aloud by a synthetic
voice. Before and after each one, the students rated their own
expectation that the treatment would work [@pmid:39177012]. Every version
raised expectations. The patient's account raised them most, and the chatbot's
least, even though the students had rated the chatbot text as moderately
clear, safe, and correctly written. Two limits. The humans appeared on video
and the machine did not, so the study cannot separate who wrote the words from
how they were delivered. And the students rated their own expectations, not a
patient's.

Put together: a tool can produce text that raters prefer and still fail to
change what a person does. The machine can draft the handout. You are the
reason the patient follows it.

### The portal reply: say a tool helped

A portal message is the secure message a patient sends the clinic through the
online system they also use to see results. Some health systems now draft a
reply before the clinician opens it.

::: {.press-clip}
<div class="src">Patient portal · illustrative message, written for this chapter</div>
<p><i>Part of this message was drafted with an automated tool and reviewed by your care team.</i></p>
<p>Hi Ms. Alvarez, thank you for letting us know about the swelling in your left ankle after starting amlodipine. Ankle swelling is a known and usually harmless side effect of this medication, and it does not mean your heart or kidneys are affected. Please continue the medication for now, keep your leg elevated when you can, and let us know if the swelling spreads above the knee, becomes painful, or is only on one side. We will review your blood pressure and the swelling at your visit on the 14th.</p>
<p>Dr. Okonkwo</p>
:::

Would you leave the italic line in? Duke surveyed 1,455 members of a patient
advisory panel. Respondents slightly *preferred* AI-drafted replies, and were
slightly *less* satisfied when told AI had been involved, by about a tenth of a
point on a five-point scale. More than three quarters were satisfied either
way [@pmid:40067301]. In follow-up interviews, 40 of those patients were
comfortable with drafted replies on one condition: a clinician reviewed them
and stayed responsible for them. They broadly supported telling patients
[@pmid:42412426].

So the label costs a little, and it is true. Leave it in; the Duke survey's
authors said the same. Some states, among them California and Texas, now
require telling patients about AI use in some cases (see Go deeper). A draft
you send is your message.

### The phone on the desk: what the patient can refuse

The tool listening to the visit is called an ambient scribe: software that
records the conversation, transcribes it, and drafts the note for the
clinician to edit and sign. It is recording the patient, so it most obviously
needs her agreement.

In a survey of UK general practitioners in August 2025, one in seven was
already using one. Of those, 63 percent routinely asked the patient's consent,
and no more than one patient in ten said no. Errors were most frequent when
more than one person was talking, when the history was complex, and when the
visit was not in English [@pmid:42386325]. So the patients most likely to be
poorly served by the note are the ones least likely to be asked in a language
they can say no in.

Which AI uses require telling the patient is not settled. What is settled is
narrower: if the tool is recording them, ask; if they ask, answer.

| The tool | Can the patient refuse it? | What you can honestly say |
|---|---|---|
| Ambient scribe recording the visit | Yes, nearly everywhere it is used; the clinician turns it off and types the note | "I can turn it off. The visit is the same either way; the note takes me longer." |
| A draft portal reply | Not usually per message; the clinician can choose to write from scratch | "I read and change every reply before it goes out, and it goes out under my name." |
| Decision support in the chart (alerts, risk scores) | No; it runs on the system, not on the patient | "That runs in the background on everyone's chart. It suggests; it does not decide." |
| AI-assisted image read | No per patient; the radiologist's read is the read | "The software marks areas for a closer look. A radiologist reads the whole study and signs it." |
| Your own use of a chatbot to look something up | Not the patient's to refuse; yours to mention if it shaped the plan | "I checked that with a reference tool and then with the guideline." |

: What can be refused, and what you can say. Institutional policy varies; the middle column is the common case, not a rule. {#tbl-decline}

"None of it, if you say so" is a comforting lie. The honest version names what
she can refuse, what she cannot, and who signs the note. That last part is
what the patient came for.

::: {.callout-important title="What you do not know about the vendor contract"}
Where the recording goes, how long it is kept, and who at the vendor can hear
it are questions about a contract you have not read. The right answer is "I
don't know how long they keep it; I'll find out, and I can turn it off today."
The wrong answer is a reassuring number you made up.

If she says no, turn it off, type the note, and write in it that the patient
declined ambient documentation.
:::

### The printout: say what is right first

A 2026 study asked five tools the same questions in a clinician's words and in
a patient's words. The patient version was worse. The share of ChatGPT's
references that were made up rose from 2.1 percent to 20.0 percent
[@pmid:42232526]. When physicians graded chatbot answers to their own
questions, most were largely right, but one in eight was mostly or completely
wrong, in the same fluent tone [@pmid:37782499]. A general-purpose chatbot writes
the most plausible next words; it does not look the answer up. So the printout's
confidence comes from the writing, not the evidence.

Telling her that is not the right first step. The order is:

**Say what is right first.** "Ferritin and thyroid function are the next two
tests I was going to order. The sleep questions are good ones." This is not a
tactic. It is true.

**Then ask what sent her there.** Almost nobody arrives with a printout because
they trust a chatbot more than a doctor. They arrive because of the last
visit. Here, the last physician gave her eight minutes and said it was probably
stress. She will not volunteer that. Ask: "What made you go looking?" A
clinician who wins the argument about the ANA and never asks has lost her
trust.

**Then the parts that are wrong, with a reason each.** "The cortisol, the Lyme
test, and the heavy metals are tests for things your story doesn't point to,
and a positive would more likely be a false one that leads to more testing.
And I'd hold off on the iron until we've measured it. If your ferritin is
normal, iron does nothing except upset your stomach, and if it's high we need
to know that too."

### The three-sentence spine

Most conversations about a tool fit three sentences in a fixed order. This
chapter calls that shape the spine. Learn the shape, not the wording.

::: {.callout-tip title="What it did. What a person did. Who is responsible."}
**What it did.** "The software marked an area on your mammogram for a closer look."

**What a person did.** "Dr. Chen read the whole study herself and agreed that area needs another picture."

**Who is responsible.** "The decision to bring you back is hers and mine, not the software's."
:::

Start with who is responsible and you sound defensive; never reach it and the
patient believes a machine decided. Keep the first two sentences separate:
patients merge "the computer flagged it" and "the radiologist agreed" into one
fact, and they are two. Say the second only when you know it is true; the
signed report tells you who read the study.

The same shape handles the phone: it listens and drafts; I read, change, and
sign; the note is mine. And the printout: the tool made a list; I am reading
it with you; the plan is ours.

When you do not know how a tool works, say so. "I don't know how that system
works, and here is how I'll find out" is a correct, professional answer. The
patient who asked about the recording does not need the retention policy in
the next ninety seconds. She needs to know you will get it, and that the visit
will not wait on it.

### Where it has already gone wrong

Patients will have read about these.

::: {.press-clips}
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">CNN Business · news</div><a class="hl" href="https://edition.cnn.com/2023/06/01/tech/eating-disorder-chatbot">National Eating Disorders Association takes its AI chatbot offline after complaints of "harmful" advice</a><div class="date">1 June 2023</div></div>
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">Norton Rose Fulbright · law-firm blog</div><a class="hl" href="https://www.insidetechlaw.com/blog/2026/08/ai-in-litigation-series-openai-sued-over-chatgpt-harmful-health-advice">AI in litigation series: OpenAI sued over ChatGPT harmful health advice</a><div class="date">11 August 2026</div></div>
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">Association of Health Care Journalists · blog</div><a class="hl" href="https://healthjournalism.org/blog/2026/02/misuse-of-ai-chatbots-in-health-care-tops-2026-health-tech-hazard-report/">Misuse of AI chatbots in health care tops 2026 Health Tech Hazard Report</a><div class="date">5 February 2026</div></div>
:::

In 2023 an eating-disorder helpline's chatbot, Tessa, gave callers weight-loss
advice: harmless for most people, harmful for the people the service existed
to help. A lawsuit filed in July 2026 alleges that a chatbot reassured a man
with weeks of dizziness. The next day he was admitted to intensive care with a
pulmonary embolism. The case has not been decided. The safety organization
ECRI named chatbot misuse its top health-technology hazard for 2026.

## Watch or listen (optional)

**Podcast.** *NEJM AI Grand Rounds*, "Partners in Diagnosis: ChatGPT, a
Mother's Intuition, and a Doctor's Expertise, with Courtney Hofmann and Dr.
Holly Gilmer" (November 20, 2024; 40 min).
<https://ai-podcast.nejm.org/e/partners-in-diagnosis-chatgpt-a-mother-s-intuition-and-a-doctor-s-expertise-with-courtney-hofman-and-dr-holly-gilmer>

After three years and many physicians, a mother put her son's records into
ChatGPT. It suggested something nobody had: tethered cord, a spinal cord held
under tension at its lower end, which surgery can correct. A pediatric
neurosurgeon confirmed it and operated. It is the printout from the other side
of the desk, with a good ending. Budget 20 minutes, which covers the
story. Listen for what sent her to a chatbot, and what Gilmer did when the
printout arrived. Then ask what this story does not show: every printout that
was wrong.

## Do

Use your university ChatGPT Edu or Copilot account. Every patient here is made
up: do not model one on someone from a rotation, and do not paste a real note,
message, or result. See [the patient information
page](../course/patient-information.qmd).

### Part A: write your sentences, then improve them (15 minutes)

Write each of these yourself first, in words you would actually say. Each
should take under a minute aloud.

1. **The phone on the desk.** The patient from the opening asks whether it is
   recording. Write the spine. Add one sentence on what she can refuse, and one
   on what you do not know and how you will find out.
2. **The computer found something.** A screening mammogram was read with
   computer-aided detection, software that marks regions for the radiologist
   to look at. It flagged a region, the radiologist agreed, and more pictures
   are recommended. A scheduler told the patient "the computer found
   something." She is 47, has not slept in two days, and will ask whether she
   has cancer. Write the spine, and the sentence that comes *before* it.
3. **The alert you cannot explain.** Pick a tool you have seen in a hospital
   and could not explain, such as a sepsis alert or a risk score. Write two
   sentences for a patient who asks how it works. The first admits you do not
   know. The second says what you will do and by when. If either reassures,
   rewrite it.

Then paste all three into your chatbot with this prompt:

```
I am a medical student practising what to say to patients about AI tools.
Below are three things I plan to say. For each one: (1) list any word a
patient with no medical training might not understand, and give a plain
word for it; (2) tell me if any sentence claims something I could not
know; (3) tell me what a frightened patient would most likely ask next.
Do not rewrite them for me.
```

Fix what you agree with. The last line is deliberate: the sentences should
sound like you, not like the chatbot.

### Part B: the printout, with a chatbot playing the patient (25 minutes) {#part-b-practice-patient}

Open a fresh conversation and paste this prompt, exactly:

> You are going to play a patient in a communication exercise for a medical
> student. Stay in character until I write STOP. You are a 34-year-old software
> developer with six weeks of fatigue. Basic labs were normal. You have brought
> two printed pages from a chatbot listing possible causes (iron deficiency,
> thyroid, sleep disorder, depression, Addison's, Lyme, EBV, heavy metals,
> autoimmune), a list of tests (ferritin, TSH, cortisol, ANA, Lyme, EBV,
> heavy metals, vitamin D, sleep study), and advice to start iron 325 mg daily
> now. You genuinely think you did useful homework and you want the tests. You
> are articulate, not embarrassed, and not hostile. Do not agree easily; push
> back at least twice if the student dismisses items without a reason. There
> is one thing you will NOT volunteer unless the student asks what made you
> look this up or what happened at your last visit: the last doctor gave you
> eight minutes and said it was probably stress. Keep each reply under 80
> words. Begin by sliding the pages across and saying you would like these
> tests.

Play the clinician, in text, for eight to ten exchanges. Then write STOP and
paste this:

> Out of character. Score me, as an observer, on each of these, with one
> sentence of evidence for each: (1) Did I find out what you already believed
> before correcting anything? (2) Did I respond to the feeling before the
> explanation? (3) Did I say which parts of the printout were right before
> which were wrong? (4) Did I ever ask what sent you to the chatbot, and did
> you tell me about the last visit? (5) Did I give a reason for each test I
> declined? (6) Did I use any jargon you would have had to guess at? (7) Did I
> leave you with one concrete next step? Then tell me the single moment you
> were most likely to stop listening.

Two warnings. A chatbot playing a patient is more agreeable than a patient; if
it gave in on the first exchange, start again with "be harder to persuade"
added. And the score is a language model's opinion of a transcript. Use it to
notice the order you spoke in, not to grade yourself.

### Keep it

```
Exchanges before I said something on the printout was right:   ___
Did I ask what sent her to the chatbot?                        Y / N
Tests I declined with a reason each:                           ___ of 6
The moment the model said she was most likely to stop listening:
_________________________________________________________________

My sentences for the phone on the desk (after Part A):
_________________________________________________________________

One thing to keep:   _____________________________________________
One thing to change: _____________________________________________
```

Bring this to your Friday small group on October 30. The week 3 cards on [the
Friday small groups page](../course/friday-groups.qmd) include the scribe
question and a caregiver who arrives with a chatbot's advice. They are the
conversations from Parts A and B, said out loud to a person. That is where you find out
whether a sentence is heard the way you meant it. To practise another card
first, change the character in the Part B prompt.

## Check

| You have | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| Sentences for the scribe (objective 1) | What it did and what you do are separate sentences, under a minute aloud; one names what she can refuse; one says what you do not know | "It helps with the note"; a made-up retention period |
| The alert you cannot explain (objective 1) | Admits what you do not know and commits to a time | Reassures |
| Who is responsible (objective 2) | A sentence with a name in it: mine, Dr. Chen's, ours | "The team," "the system," or no sentence |
| The sentence before the mammogram spine (objective 2) | Responds to the fear before explaining the software | Starts with "the software" |
| The Part B transcript (objective 3) | Something right named before anything wrong; you asked what sent her; each declined test has a reason | Won the argument; never asked; "we don't need those" |
| The empathy finding (objective 4) | You can say why text raters prefer can still persuade less, and name one limit of each study | "AI is more empathetic" or "AI is cold" |
| Kept sentences (objective 5) | You changed what the chatbot flagged that you agreed with, and the sentences still sound like you | Pasted a rewrite, or nothing kept |

## What this changes for you

*What does this change about how you'll practice?* Write it down in two parts.
First, the sentence you will say to the first patient who asks whether a
computer was involved in their care; not the shape, the sentence. Second, go
back to the desk. The phone is still listening and the two pages are still in
front of you. In what order do you answer her two questions, and what is the
first thing you say about the pages? If it is a correction, start again.

## Summary

- Raters called chatbot text more empathetic; in another study, the same kind
  of text changed expectations least. You are the reason a patient follows the
  handout.
- Patients slightly prefer AI-drafted replies and are slightly less satisfied
  when told. Tell them anyway.
- The scribe can be refused; the alert in the chart cannot. Say which, say what
  you do not know, and say whose note it is.
- With a printout: say what is right first, ask what sent them, then give a
  reason for each no.
- What it did; what a person did; who is responsible. In that order.
- A chatbot is a good practice patient. Friday is where you say it to a person.

## Go deeper

**Papers**

- The empathy study [@pmid:37115527] and its repeat with the reasons coded
  [@pmid:41359230]. The repeat also found that participants rated a response
  as more empathetic when told a physician wrote it, whether or not one had.
- The Zurich course, for the persuasion experiment and for teaching students to
  judge patient-facing text [@pmid:39177012].
- The two Duke studies on AI-drafted portal messages, the survey
  [@pmid:40067301] and the interviews [@pmid:42412426]; together the best
  current evidence on what patients want to be told and when.
- What drafts do for clinicians. At Stanford, in the first weeks after one tool
  was introduced, clinicians used the draft about a fifth of the time and
  reported less workload and exhaustion, with no change in how long a reply
  took [@pmid:38506805]. At UC San Diego, where clinics were switched on at
  random, drafts made replies 18 percent longer and did not shorten the time to
  write them [@pmid:38619840].
- The UK scribe survey [@pmid:42386325], and a short argument for
  patient-centred consent to ambient recording [@pmid:42399409].
- A 2019 nationally representative US survey, before chatbots: two thirds of
  respondents said it was very important to be told when AI played a big role
  in their diagnosis or treatment [@pmid:35507346].
- The clinician-versus-patient prompt comparison [@pmid:42232526]; the tools
  were also more likely to cite websites rather than papers.

**The state laws.** Since January 2025, California has required a disclaimer
on generative-AI messages about a patient's clinical care unless a licensed
clinician read and reviewed them. Since September 2025, Texas has required a
practitioner who uses AI for diagnosis to tell the patient and to review what
the AI wrote. Since January 2026, a second Texas law has required anyone
providing health care to say when a patient is interacting with an AI system,
by the date of the first service.

**Listen**

- *Tradeoffs*, "Should I Trust AI to Diagnose Me?" (October 30, 2025; 25 min),
  with physician and writer Dhruv Khullar, which adds the argument that
  relying on the tool weakens your own skill
